pr_title: Disallow certs with explicit curve in verification chain
pr_body:
The check is applied with X509_V_FLAG_X509_STRICT.

Fixes #12139

##### Checklist
<!-- Remove items that do not apply. For completed items, change [ ] to [x]. -->
- [x] documentation is added or updated
- [x] tests are added or updated
pr_comments: @mspncp Does this affect your use case?

We need a new property somewhere: at the moment we have nothing that keeps track of how the source material encoded the parameters. The `asn1_flag` field in 1.1.1 and in master only tracks what the user wants in output (and defaults to named curve) but does not not always match what the original encoding was!
You're saying it does not work but it works by my local testing. So where is the discrepancy coming from?

If it is currently working correctly in all corner cases, it is by accident and not by design, that is what I meant.

That flag, by design, is supposed to track how the key owner wants to encode the parameters at serialization.
The value it takes by default, and what different codepaths in how the key material gets actually parsed, what the user code programmatically does to manipulate that flag after the key has been parsed are all things that might effect the result of the testing.

In the end it comes down to read a flag that has one meaning ("how should I encode this on output?") as if it had a different semantic value ("how was this encoded on input? "), and is potentially calling for unexpected behavior.

Even if it works in all cases _currently_, overloading the flag with double semantic should also be considered a breaking behavioral change as it might lead to hard to debug issues for user code!
@romen, would you be please able to propose a PR that would add a proper flag then?

> You're saying it does not work but it works by my local testing. So where is the discrepancy coming from?

Most places just leave this option alone so it will just have a named curve flag value of 1 . A named curve can however set this flag to 0 (explicit) so that if it is written out to der/pem it will use explicit form. That is what the flag is really for.
Hijacking it for something else because it 'appears to work' is not a good idea :).

If we still decide to go ahead and overload that flag meaning, we definitely need to put a note in the validation code about how that flag is being interpreted, and document very clearly the change of meaning in the flag and under what conditions it must reflect what was read instead of what should be written.

The thing is there is already third party code depending on the flag being set "properly" when the certificates are read. So I am afraid it is too late (or rather it would be actually a hidden API break) if we decided to not set the flag appropriately during decoding.

> if we still decide to go ahead and overload that flag meaning, we definitely need to put a note in the validation code about how that flag is being interpreted, and document very clearly the change of meaning in the flag and under what conditions it must reflect what was read instead of what should be written.

Lets not do that.. I think it needs to be a seperate concept. The "encoding" is already being used by the explicit curve code that I added - and it means the same as it did before.

But as I said - at least in case of decoding EC pub keys from certificates the flag is already set depending on the encoding used in the certificate and changing this would break API compatibility. So yes, I have no problem with adding another "alias" flag but I do not think we should actively drop the code setting this existing flag from the eckey_type2param()

> The thing is there is already third party code depending on the flag being set "properly" when the certificates are read. So I am afraid it is too late (or rather it would be actually a hidden API break) if we decided to not set the flag appropriately during decoding.

Do you have examples? 
It is also weird nobody opened an issue about it yet, because in 1.0.2 that flag defaulted to explicit unless otherwise changed, in 1.1.1 the default changed to named if possible and unless otherwise set, and then always in 1.1.1, during the past year as a security fix, we also have code that detects explicit parameters matching known curves and treats them internally exactly as if parsed with the curve OID.

All of this was possible because that flag referred to what to do on output not what was read on input. That is why I think we would need a separate flag tracking only what happened on input and a new getter.

What is the right place to implement this property I do not know: clearly it is not a key property in the "provider" sense of it (it is not one of its domain parameters, secret or public values, nor a parameter conditioning the key usage/capabilities). It looks more like a property of the decode context to be read separately from the returned EVP_PKEY object contents.
Here is the example: https://lightshipsec.com/explicitly-parameterized-ecdsa-x-509-certificates/
Also quick search for OPENSSL_EC_NAMED_CURVE gives for example: https://stackoverflow.com/questions/24247371/identify-ec-curve-in-certificate-using-openssl-api

> Here is the example: https://lightshipsec.com/explicitly-parameterized-ecdsa-x-509-certificates/

OK, luckily this recommendation is only 1 month old, we could contact them and inform them that the usage of the flag in that use case is potentially wrong, before it spreads to stack overflow and ends up in applications.

The fact that it is a new standardized requirement with security implications, makes me think we should consider opening first a PR that optionally let users activate the strict check in 1.1.1 and then forward port that change to 3.0.0 rather than trying to fix this in 3.0.0 and back port it. (In 3.0 strict could be the new default, but we should have an option of non strictness for legacy applications probably?)
The requirement was there in the RFC from the start. So it is not anything new. It just started now to be enforced by NIAP certifications.
Also saying the use of the flag is wrong, when it apparently works and there is no "truly right" alternative apart from parsing the certificate yourself is kind of moot exercise.

> Also quick search for OPENSSL_EC_NAMED_CURVE gives for example: https://stackoverflow.com/questions/24247371/identify-ec-curve-in-certificate-using-openssl-api

While the code refers clearly to 1.0.2, technically that SO answer is not wrong (but can be misleading), it does not say "if named_curve is set the certificate was encoded with explicit parameters", if the flag is set to named one can indeed use get_curve_name(), because in that case it is guaranteed that the group has an associated name.
Also, for named curves one can still get all the explicit curve parameters too, so even the last part of the answer is not wrong.

What is misleading is assuming that the value of that flag reflects what was encoded in the parsed data: that was never its meaning, and not having a need for this functionality, simply there is no mechanism in 1.0.2 or 1.1.1 to reveal how the key was originally encoded.

Should we then drop the  EC_GROUP_set_asn1_flag calls from EC_GROUP_new_from_ecpkparameters function? Because that ensures that the mechanism exists (for public keys only and unless you override the value of the flag by a subsequent call of course).

I do not mean that seriously though.

> Also saying the use of the flag is wrong, when it apparently works and there is no "truly right" alternative apart from parsing the certificate yourself is kind of moot exercise.

That is exactly why I am thinking we should propose a working alternative to get this new information in 1.1.1,and then forward port it to 3.0. I expect applications that will stay for 1.1.1 with the duration of its support to require this for conformance and security reasons, which would qualify this "new feature" as a security fix (one could also spin the "missing getter" argument, saying we miss a getter that tells us something about a characteristic of the parsed asn1 data).

(by the way, the fact that we override explicit encodings for builtin curves and that we mock with that flag value for output is exactly to prevent the risks for which the current recommendation is to avoid explicit parameters altogether)

Until the past year the logic was quite simple and lended itself nicely for "abusing/misinterpreting" the flag as referring to what was read rather than what is meant to be output:

> if input data had explicit paras, set output flag to explicit params; if input data has named curve set output flag to named curve

Then for the same (and more) reasons the RFC discourages explicit parameters in certificates, we decided to make sure that when a key is read (even outside of a certificate) an attacker cannot use a (supported, and used by default in keys generated in 1.0.2) explicit parameters encoding to bypass all the security hardening (and collaterally performance gains) that went in for built-in curves and that have different level of safety (and performance hit) on generic curves.

Now the code that reads keys and parameters is not used solely in certificate parsing, and the requirement to reject input encoded in explicit form is strictly limited to certificate parsing: overloading the meaning of that flag for this (very important) use case seems hazardous, but given how important (and relevant for our users) it is to get a clear answer on "how was the data encoded?" I would suggest to have a dedicated mechanism to be applied in 1.1.1 and 3.0.0 (and I expect 3rd party vendors that are still offering support for 1.0.2 might also want to backport such functionality)
Should we just have a flag in the certificate itself (or rather in the X509_PUBKEY). Although I can think of usefulness of the flag in other contexts as well it would be IMO a bigger fish to fry.
I've added a new flag to EC_KEY flags. When setting it I still depend on the ASN.1 group flag being set but that's just temporarily.
This also seems to fix #12139
Does this flag need to be set in EC_GROUP_new_from_params() also?

The question is what would be the usefulness of the tri-state flag value. For this particular case the indicator of the explicit encoding is sufficient, with both remaining states being coalesced into one. Do you have any other use-case on mind?

> The question is what would be the usefulness of the tri-state flag value. For this particular case the indicator of the explicit encoding is sufficient, with both remaining states being coalesced into one. Do you have any other use-case on mind?

Not sure about a use case outside of the need for x509 validation, but if this is going into the public EC API we need to make sure its semantic is clear and we don't have undocumented undefined behavior.

Having an undefined state could help preventing the ambiguity of the case in which no _decoding_ was involved for the group of this key, yet that group was created by specifiying parameters and not a curve OID.

We should probably add tests anyway for the expected results in the "otherwise" case, to improve coverage of the new API and prevent our implementation from behaving differently from the definition.

Inside the X509 validation code we are testing here, as far as I can tell, an `EC_KEY` object usually has a single point of origin and goes through this:

_X509 decoder_
-> _ASN1 key decoder_ (returns an `EC_KEY` containing the freshly built `EC_GROUP` from following calls)
-> `d2i_ECPKParameters()` (returns `EC_GROUP`)
-> `EC_GROUP_new_from_ecpkparameters()` (returns `EC_GROUP`)
-> `EC_GROUP_new_from_ecparameters()` (returns `EC_GROUP`)

`EC_GROUP_new_from_ecpkparameters()` is the one that parses the actual encoding and differentiates between _named curve OID_ or _explicit params_, so it makes sense to set the new flag in here, but the caveat is that only when the caller is `d2i_ECPKParameters()` (like in the X509 use case) we can guarantee something about the original encoding.

The current definition says

> `EC_KEY_is_from_explicit_encoding()` returns `1` if the group of the key was decoded from explicitly encoded group parameters, and `0` otherwise.

According to this, in all the cases in which `EC_GROUP_new_from_ecpkparameters()` detects _explicit params_, if the caller is not `d2i_ECPKParameters()` we should fall in the "otherwise" case.  This policy is not really easy to implement: `EC_GROUP_new_from_ecpkparameters()` can see if the passed encoding was explicit params or OID, but `d2i_ECPKParameters()` is the one that knows if the `ecpkparameters` have been decoded.

What should the API return if this `EC_KEY` object was created from an `EC_GROUP`

- returned by `d2i_ECPKParameters()`?
  - current definition would say: `1` if input was encoded with explicit parameters, `0` if input was encoded with a named curve
  - current implementation matches (and is the only one tested)
- returned by `EC_GROUP_new_from_ecpkparameters()` that received its input from another object `EC_GROUP_get_ecpkparameters()`? (the retrieved `ECPKPARAMETERS` type can be _named_ or _explicit_, depending on the source object ASN1 **output** flag, it does not depend on the value of the new flag of the source object)
  - no decoding happened for the group of the key object passed to `EC_KEY_is_from_explicit_encoding()`, so we should return `0` as per the _otherwise_ case, independently from what the `ECPKPARAMETERS` used to create the group of this key looked like. Is this interpretation too strict? (does the ambiguity warrant a note in the documentation to clarify this?)
  - I expect the current implementation is returning `1` if the source object had its output flag set to _explicit params_, which **violates a strict interpretation** of the current definition
- returned by `EC_GROUP_new_from_ecparameters()` that received its input from another object `EC_GROUP_get_ecparameters()`? (the retrieved `ECPARAMETERS` are always explicit)
  - no decoding happened for the group of the key object passed to `EC_KEY_is_from_explicit_encoding()`, so we should return `0` as per the _otherwise_ case. Is this interpretation too strict?
  - in the current implementation, we are not setting the new flag in `EC_GROUP_new_from_ecparameters()`, so we should always be returning `0` in this case, which is compatible with the strict interpretation of the current definition
- created with `EC_GROUP_new_curve_GFp()` or `EC_GROUP_new_curve_GF2m()` or `EC_GROUP_new(); EC_GROUP_set_curve()`, with parameters matching a known named curve?
  - no decoding is happening, so we would expect always `0`?
  - current implementation never touches the new flag in this case, so, as long as `EC_GROUP_new()` initializes the flag to `0`, we are compliant with the strict interpretation
- created with `EC_GROUP_new_curve_GFp()` or `EC_GROUP_new_curve_GF2m()` or `EC_GROUP_new(); EC_GROUP_set_curve()`, with parameters _not_ matching a known named curve?
  - no decoding is happening, so we would expect always `0`?
  - current implementation never touches the new flag in this case, so, as long as `EC_GROUP_new()` initializes the flag to `0`, we are compliant with the strict interpretation
- created with `EC_GROUP_new_by_curve_name()`?
  - no decoding is happening, so we would expect always `0`?
  - current implementation never touches the new flag in this case, so, as long as `EC_GROUP_new()` initializes the flag to `0`, we are compliant with the strict interpretation

Above I said:

> Inside the X509 validation code we are testing here, as far as I can tell, an `EC_KEY` object usually has a single point of origin

What is the expected behavior of the X509 validation code for X509 objects created from scratch and filled with an `EC_KEY` created from any of the "no decoding happened" cases above?

> We should probably add tests anyway for the expected results in the "otherwise" case, to improve coverage of the new API and prevent our implementation from behaving differently from the definition.

Yes, I'll add tests once we come to some final conclusion about the API semantics.
 
>     * returned by `EC_GROUP_new_from_ecpkparameters()` that received its input from another object `EC_GROUP_get_ecpkparameters()`? (the retrieved `ECPKPARAMETERS` type can be _named_ or _explicit_, depending on the source object ASN1 **output** flag, it does not depend on the value of the new flag of the source object)
>       
>       * no decoding happened for the group of the key object passed to `EC_KEY_is_from_explicit_encoding()`, so we should return `0` as per the _otherwise_ case, independently from what the `ECPKPARAMETERS` used to create the group of this key looked like. Is this interpretation too strict? (does the ambiguity warrant a note in the documentation to clarify this?)
>       * I expect the current implementation is returning `1` if the source object had its output flag set to _explicit params_, which **violates a strict interpretation** of the current definition

True. However there was actually a decoding of ECPARAMETERS happenning. So the question is whether just documenting this would be sufficient or whether you think that this is really misleading behaviour of the flag - it would have to be somehow set in the d2i function only. @romen what would be your preference?
 
>     * returned by `EC_GROUP_new_from_ecparameters()` that received its input from another object `EC_GROUP_get_ecparameters()`? (the retrieved `ECPARAMETERS` are always explicit)
>       
>       * no decoding happened for the group of the key object passed to `EC_KEY_is_from_explicit_encoding()`, so we should return `0` as per the _otherwise_ case. Is this interpretation too strict?
>       * in the current implementation, we are not setting the new flag in `EC_GROUP_new_from_ecparameters()`, so we should always be returning `0` in this case, which is compatible with the strict interpretation of the current definition

Actually no, we set the flag in EC_GROUP_new_from_ecparameters() as of now. We could easily move the setting to the EC_GROUP_new_from_ecpkparameters but that would not make it more consistent.

>     * created with `EC_GROUP_new_curve_GFp()` or `EC_GROUP_new_curve_GF2m()` or `EC_GROUP_new(); EC_GROUP_set_curve()`, with parameters matching a known named curve?
>       
>       * no decoding is happening, so we would expect always `0`?
>       * current implementation never touches the new flag in this case, so, as long as `EC_GROUP_new()` initializes the flag to `0`, we are compliant with the strict interpretation

Yes, this case is fine. But yes, there should be a test.

>     * created with `EC_GROUP_new_curve_GFp()` or `EC_GROUP_new_curve_GF2m()` or `EC_GROUP_new(); EC_GROUP_set_curve()`, with parameters _not_ matching a known named curve?
>       
>       * no decoding is happening, so we would expect always `0`?
>       * current implementation never touches the new flag in this case, so, as long as `EC_GROUP_new()` initializes the flag to `0`, we are compliant with the strict interpretation

Yes, as above.

>     * created with `EC_GROUP_new_by_curve_name()`?
>       
>       * no decoding is happening, so we would expect always `0`?
>       * current implementation never touches the new flag in this case, so, as long as `EC_GROUP_new()` initializes the flag to `0`, we are compliant with the strict interpretation

Yes, as above.

> Above I said:
> 
> > Inside the X509 validation code we are testing here, as far as I can tell, an `EC_KEY` object usually has a single point of origin
> 
> What is the expected behavior of the X509 validation code for X509 objects created from scratch and filled with an `EC_KEY` created from any of the "no decoding happened" cases above?

I do not even think the X509 chain verification would work properly on any X509 objects created from scratch. But perhaps the check in the verification code should include also EC_GROUP_get_curve_name(grp) == NID_undef as a second condition to make it somewhat more consistent.
Ping @romen

@romen Do you prefer setting the flag only when real decoding happens via d2i_ECPKParameters or do you prefer to keep it as is but document that EC_GROUP_new_from_...parameters set it?
IMO there is implicit decoding happening when these functions are called so it makes sense this way as well, but I am also OK with making the flag more strictly defined.

Sorry @t8m , I am running late on too many things.

Maybe it works with setting it only on `d2i_ECParameters` (which means implicitly a decoding is actually happening), and be more explicit in the documentation about the caveats of what we mean by decoding?

I don't want to block this further because at the moment I can't really follow-up in a timely manner! (Apologies again!)

> @mspncp Does this affect your use case?

No, in my case the curves are used for ECDH only. 

_(Sorry @slontis for my late response, I missed your question.)_
This is now really waiting on reviews.
I would argue that this doesnt fix the bug which states the problem in 1_1_1 and 1_0_2.. Do you plan on a separate PR for 111?
This is so much better that the first pass.. Good job.

> I would argue that this doesnt fix the bug which states the problem in 1_1_1 and 1_0_2.. Do you plan on a separate PR for 111?

Yep, I'd like to do separate PR for 111. Ideally it would be just a trivial backport. However there is the question whether having this check applied only on auth level >= 1 is sufficient or whether we want to make it optional even more (perhaps based on the strict verify flag)?
This pull request is ready to merge

When resolving the conflict I realized that enabling the check based on SECLEVEL is probably not ideal. @DDvO should I instead base it on the X509_V_FLAG_X509_STRICT? Hopefully it is OK if I put it to check_chain_extensions along the other strict checks.

> When resolving the conflict I realized that enabling the check based on SECLEVEL is probably not ideal. 
>@DDvO should I instead base it on the X509_V_FLAG_X509_STRICT? Hopefully it is OK if I put it to check_chain_extensions along the other strict checks.

What is the motivation of disallowing certs with explicit curves?
When I understand this better I hopefully can give a more informed response,
but making the new check depend on X509_V_FLAG_X509_STRICT sounds reasonable.
It is RFC 5480 Section 2.1.1 requirement.
@slontis can you please re-review? @DDvO or you?

> It is RFC 5480 Section 2.1.1 requirement.

I see. Then doing this check when X509_V_FLAG_X509_STRICT is set is the right thing.

> @slontis can you please re-review? @DDvO or you?

I've started my review,~~but it won't be sufficient for approval~~...
@DDvO comments addressed.

> @DDvO comments addressed.

Thanks for your quick reaction.
We're moving house yesterday, today, and tomorrow, that's why I did not see it until now.
I'm expecting that you add a test with a real certificate that you want to reject.

According to the manpage, EC_GROUP_get_asn1_flag can return OPENSSL_EC_NAMED_CURVE or OPENSSL_EC_EXPLICIT_CURVE, where OPENSSL_EC_EXPLICIT_CURVE is 0. I think it would make sense to compare the return value against the define.
I am afraid that I won't have time to "perfectionalize" :smile: this in the next few days so it will not make it to beta.

> I am afraid that I won't have time to "perfectionalize" smile this in the next few days so it will not make it to beta.

I understand. BTW, when earliest will feature freeze actually happen?
So how if I re-approve now, we merge tomorrow, and I will try to address the open issues in a new PR, say, by Wednesday?
If this does not work out, we can still  convert the open points into an issue to be solved later.

In fact as this is basically a bug fix (RFC conformance fix) I believe this could be merged post beta. (We are even going to backport to 1.1.1 although there I'd definitely make the check conditional on strict verify param.)

issue_context.title: OpenSSL should disallow custom elliptic curves in certificate chains.
issue_context.body:
### Affected Versions
1.1.1g, 1.0.2u

### Setup
OpenSSL has been compiled from source in an alpine docker container. The following excerpt of the used docker file shows the build related commands:
```
RUN ./config --prefix=/build/ --openssldir=/build/ no-async 
RUN make -s && make install_sw -s
```
After building it the respective OpenSSL version and required libraries have been copied into an minimal docker container (from scratch).

The server is later started using the following command:
`openssl s_server -accept 4433 -Verify 100 -cert /cert/inputCerts/rootv3.pem -key /cert/keys/rootv3.pem -CAfile /cert/inputCerts/root.pem -verify_return_error`

All files mentioned in this report (certificates, keys, etc.) have been included in the attached zip archive.

### Issue
OpenSSL allows certificate chains in which custom elliptic curves are used. The recent Curveball vulnerability in Windows leads to the question if this should be allows. I think to prevent any mishaps from occurring this shouldn't be allowed by default. As far as I'm aware any public certificate chains use named curves so this *shouldn't* cause any incompatibilities.

### Reproduction
Uses OpenSSL 1.1.1 client on Ubuntu 18.04.
Connect to the started server using the following command:
`openssl s_client -connect localhost:4433 -cert ECROOTv3_CAv3CustomCurve_LEAF_ECv3__leaf_certificate1.pem -key eckey_secp256r1_3.pem -CAfile ECROOTv3_CAv3CustomCurve_LEAF_ECv3__ca_certificate1.pem`

### Expected Result
OpenSSL should reject the certificate chain since custom elliptic curves bear more security concerns than gains.

### Actual Result
OpenSSL happily accepts the certificate and proceeds with the handshake.

### Attachment
[opensslCustomEC.zip](https://github.com/openssl/openssl/files/4774643/opensslCustomEC.zip)
comments:
Would disabling this by default in 1.1.1 create a risk for people that built their own CA and PKI using openssl versions where the default encoding was with explicit parameters?

If the above risk is considerable, I think a version of #12683 is desirable in 1.1.1, but maybe as an opt in? 
This is clear violation of RFC5280 but yes, for 1.1.1 we need to consider the conditions under which the check is enabled.
@kroeckx could you please check your cert database if you see there any intermediates with explicitly encoded ECDSA parameters?
I don't really have a check for that currently. I have a list of
allowed nids, those allowed by the BRs: NID_X9_62_prime256v1,
NID_secp384r1, NID_secp521r1

I think that check would trigger such certs, but I'm not sure. But
it will clearly trigger on certs using brainpool.

If you have an example certs and tell me how to detect it, I'd be
happy to make x509lint check that, and run it over the database.
I guess I should just have looked at your PR and used the
EC_GROUP_get_asn1_flag()
Or reading it again, that might also not work?
I think I can see it using X509_PUBKEY_get0_param ...

x509lint has been updated, processing the databasa, so far nothing
found.
So I found some, but so far they're all weird.
The EC_GROUP_get_asn1_flag() works, although accidentally only.
Let's reopen as we want to fix it also on 1.1.1 branch.
This is now also fixed in 1.1.1, so closing.

> 
> If the above risk is considerable, I think a version of #12683 is desirable in 1.1.1, but maybe as an opt in?

This did happen to my home setup - I updated and started getting this error out of nginx. For others who come to this issue, specify `-param_enc named_curve` when generating with `openssl ecparam`.

review_comments:
Can I be annoying a little longer and propose to have a comment before each test that explicitly describes conditions and expectations?

I won't hold my approval if this is not done, it's just a suggestion.
OK, done.
Should we have an accessor for EC_GROUP as well and test that instead?
We should also have tests for the behavior of the EC_KEY_decoded_from_explicit_params wrapper.
No, I would like to avoid adding more API calls and the users are simplified by the existing EC_KEY wrapper. IMO the existing accessor should be sufficient. I'll add the test for the wrapper.

Ok about not adding the extra accessor to the public API if you don't think it is needed beyond testing.
This matter i consider resolved.

What is unresolved is the fact that we test the internal behavior of the flag inside EC_GROUP but we are missing tests for the public API to ensure it conforms to our documentation.
But I added the EC_KEY_decoded_from_explicit_params() to the test code. Is there something else missing?

Yes... That I can't read anymore! 🤦‍♂️

Sorry for the noise!

Actually this and the new public function seems not needed if you generalize the check because RFC 5480 forbids also implicitCurve:
`check_curve()` could simply check if  `curve_name` contains a valid NID, which would imply not implicit and not explicit parameters, right?

Nope, that would not work as the curve name is set also for keys that have explicit params that matches one of the named curves. And as the implicit parameters are not supported at all, they do not need to be flagged this way. I'd like to keep this as is.
I see

> that would not work as the curve name is set also for keys that have explicit params that matches one of the named curves. And as the implicit parameters are not supported at all, they do not need to be flagged this way. 

Hmm, since this PR is still under discussion I'd like to revisit this point.
If a named curve happens to match a predefined curve I'd say this does not need to be flagged as wrong because the essence of the RFC requirement is that 'custom` curves must not be used.

I tentatively did the following simple change:
```
diff --git a/crypto/x509/x509_vfy.c b/crypto/x509/x509_vfy.c
index b7afdbbccb..046518d8ae 100644
--- a/crypto/x509/x509_vfy.c
+++ b/crypto/x509/x509_vfy.c
@@ -3460,7 +3460,7 @@ static int check_curve(X509 *cert)
         return 1;
 
     if (EVP_PKEY_id(pkey) == EVP_PKEY_EC
-        && EC_KEY_decoded_from_explicit_params(EVP_PKEY_get0_EC_KEY(pkey)))
+        && EC_GROUP_get_curve_name(EC_KEY_get0_group(EVP_PKEY_get0_EC_KEY(pkey))) != NID_undef)
         return 0;
 #endif
 
```
and the tests still pass. Yet this is no wonder since there is no test with a certificate having an implicit or explicit curve.
I still have the impression that the function `EC_KEY_decoded_from_explicit_params()` is not really needed.
RFC5480 says: `implicitCurve and specifiedCurve MUST NOT be used in PKIX.` So the only option is that namedCurve is used.

So the question is on how strict we want to enforce that. The CABForum has in it's BRs: "The parameters MUST use the namedCurve encoding.", and then exact bytes for each of the allowed curves.

I have yet to find the first real certificate that doesn't use the namedCurve. The only ones I've seen have been converted from namedCurve and then fail the signature check, or test certificates to show what should get rejected.
